Executive Summary
At Least 85% of U.S. Funeral Home Locations Remain Independent
12,531 tracked independent locations face a tracked consolidated footprint of 2,149 locations, five groups holding 85.2% of it, a retirement wave, and a cremation shift that rewards early scale.
The STOC View
Deathcare has been consolidating for sixty years, and the wave stalled: after the 1990s roll-up race ended in Loewen’s bankruptcy and years of SCI divestitures, the buyer side concentrated instead of spreading, and five groups now hold 85.2% of the tracked consolidated footprint, SCI alone 60.9%. The result is a $23.9B industry (IBISWorld) in which at least 85% of locations are still independent (chains over-index on revenue through combos and pre-need), with, in most markets, no tracked institutional buyer other than SCI, if that. Part of that vacuum is selectivity, since the majors buy where combos and growth demographics clear their overhead; the rest is open to a buyer whose cost structure clears where the majors’ does not: Pennsylvania’s 919 independents face 32 tracked chain locations; even Texas, SCI’s home state, is 84.9% independent after a full directory count. What makes this cycle different from the 1990s is the seller side, met by a small field of disciplined buyers where the last cycle had competing leveraged roll-ups. Roughly half of owners told NFDA’s 2023 survey they plan to retire by 2028, and cremation, at 62.8% of 2025 dispositions, is compressing revenue per call faster than single-site operators can restructure, turning a fragmented owner base into motivated sellers. The play is therefore to leave SCI’s dense markets alone and become the second institutional buyer in the rest: deep-supply, lightly consolidated, cremation-forward metros, entered through multi-location independents, before the retirement wave meets today’s thin institutional buyer field.

Market Implications
1
Enter the whitespace before the majors’ next cycle
Colorado (45.7% tracked-chain share) and Arizona (41.7%) show what a market looks like where the combo-and-growth playbook has already run; the deepest pools show the opposite: Pennsylvania holds 919 independents at a 96.6% runway, Illinois 633 at 92.4%, and Texas, once counted against full national directories, 1,158 at 84.9%. The map on page 7 and the state table on page 8 show that split for every market.
2
Build first where independents already market cremation
Dallas-Fort Worth (73.2% of scrape independents cremation-visible), Charlotte (65.2%), and Riverside (64.3%) lead the 16 cremation-forward deep pools (metro scrape bases on page 5), where direct-cremation entrants already compete on price. Cremation-visible measures marketing posture on independents’ own websites; Texas’s statewide disposition mix still trails the national cremation rate on NFDA state data, and margin defense in these markets rewards scaled platforms first. The traditional-mix pools remain the scale play once a cremation-capable platform exists. Detail on pages 5 and 10.
3
Anchor on the 215 scrape-observed multi-location independents, sourced through succession
They run 536 observed locations, with the largest tracked clusters in Baltimore (46 multi-site locations) and Washington (29); the counts are floors and unevenly detected across metros (detail on page 9). Anchors bring management, licensure coverage, and local brand equity a new platform cannot build quickly. NFDA’s 2023 owner survey put roughly half of owners on a retire-by-2028 timeline, and 42% of those without exit plans would consider selling for the right offer, so a proprietary succession pipeline beats waiting for auctions. Segmentation follows on page 9.

Industry size: IBISWorld Funeral Homes in the US, accessed August 2026. Cremation rate: CANA 2026 Annual Statistics Report, May 2026; trajectory: NFDA 2025 Cremation and Burial Report, October 2025. Priority Consolidation Markets
Thirty-Four Metros Hold Deep Independent Pools, and Sixteen of Them Are Already Cremation-Forward
Transparent, sequential rules on classified independent depth and cremation-visible mix; every metro lands in exactly one group.
Part I: Thesis and Priority Markets
Across 840 observed CBSAs (metropolitan and micropolitan areas), 34 clear 50 or more independent locations each and together hold 4,207 independents, 33.6% of the independent base. The split that matters for sequencing is the cremation-visible mix: 16 of the 34 are at or above 50%, and 18 remain traditional-weighted, led by New York, Philadelphia, and Pittsburgh, three of the four largest pools in the country. San Antonio enters the deep-pool tier on the Texas directory census, and Houston and Dallas-Fort Worth deepen from roughly 50 to roughly 190 independents each on it; Boston (216), Providence (72), Hartford (50), and the New Jersey sides of the New York and Philadelphia metros enter on the Northeast ZIP repair (Methodology).

Cremation-Visible = share of the metro’s scrape independents with a visible cremation offering on their own websites: a visibility signal only (directory-census records carry no service signals, so Texas rates rest on thin scrape bases: San Antonio 20, Houston 52, Dallas-Fort Worth 56). Multi-Site Indep. = locations run by independent operators with two or more locations; domain-grouped counts are floors and uneven across metros, and Texas zeros are structural, since directory-census records carry no operator identity. Tracked Chains = named-group locations carrying this metro’s code; 1,580 of the 2,149 tracked consolidated locations carry a metro code, so metro consolidated counts are floors of chain presence and metro shares on average understate it; state-level shares, which carry the full roster, govern (Methodology).
Group A: build where independents already market the mix
Dallas-Fort Worth (73.2% cremation-visible, 188 independents on the full Texas count), Charlotte (65.2%), Riverside (64.3%), and San Francisco (63.8%) lead the cremation-visible mixes. San Antonio joins the tier on the census and Houston deepens to 192 independents; direct-cremation brands are already present in these markets, and scaled platforms defend margin best.
Group B: the biggest pools, the slowest mix
New York (683 independents, 42.9% cremation-visible), Philadelphia (320, 40.9%), and Pittsburgh (234, 47.9%) hold three of the four deepest pools in the country with a burial-weighted mix, larger books per call today and a longer conversion runway.
Key Read: Depth, mix, and consolidation all diverge. Four of the five largest pools are traditional-weighted Northeast metros, while Chicago, the second largest, tips cremation-forward and holds Group A’s largest pool, alongside Sun Belt and mid-continent metros; tracked chain presence inside Group A runs from 55 locations in Houston and 40 in Miami down to 9 in Baltimore, with Chicago’s 23 the lowest share at 6.1% (metro counts are floors; state shares govern). The full Texas count shows what thin coverage had hidden: Houston and Dallas-Fort Worth hold deep pools of roughly 190 independents each at 22.3% and 14.2% tracked-chain share. A sponsor sequencing both plays enters long-runway Group A metros first for margin defense and Group B for scale.
Source. STOC Advisory proprietary CBSA market analysis, August 2026 (roster-reconciled ownership). Denominators: 12,592 CBSA-assigned records; group rules printed above; cremation-visible shares use each metro’s scrape independents.

Current Platform and Sponsor Landscape
Five Groups Own 85.2% of All Tracked Chain Locations, and SCI Alone Owns 60.9%
2,149 tracked named-group locations, roster-reconciled, 14.6% of dataset records, across 20 observed groups; footprints reconciled against company directories
Part I: Thesis and Priority Markets
The tracked consolidated footprint is 2,149 locations, 14.6% of the 14,680-record universe, across the 20 observed groups, and it is a pyramid: five groups hold 85.2% of it, the next seven hold another 12.7%, and everything else is regional. Location rosters harvested from the major groups’ own directories (2,143 roster rows, including SCI’s full consumer directory) were matched against the scrape, reclassifying 466 records collected as independent targets; the 1,450 roster locations the scrape had missed were added as records. The largest chain footprints now mirror the companies’ own directories: SCI shows 1,308 funeral-service locations against its reported 1,495 at June 30, 2026 (the gap is cemetery-side directory pages and directory lag; verified funeral-home combos are retained). The 26-group crosswalk on page 13 is the source of truth on ownership claims.

Bar length scales to the state’s classified total (Texas, 1,364, sets the full width); the split shows independent vs tracked chains. Runway = independent share of classified locations. SCI leads the tracked-chain column in 36 of the 50 state markets with tracked chain presence (Delaware shows none); Park Lawn, Vertin, Milestone, NorthStar and FPG lead the remainder, three small states tied. Where runway is long and supply deep, a platform builds free of an entrenched national’s footprint and pre-need book, though nationals can still bid in.

Independent Operator Base
Four Segments Sort the 11,585 Independents by Who to Call First
Multi-location operators, high-visibility singles, the cremation-visible pool, and the deeper-research remainder; each location in exactly one segment
Part III: The Independent Opportunity
The 11,585 scrape-observed independent locations resolve into 11,264 operators through validated website and business-identity grouping; operators that share no website domain resolve as separate singles, so multi-site counts are floors, and unevenly so across metros (branch chapels on separate domains resolve as singles). Segments are assigned sequentially: operating scale first, then public visibility, then cremation capability, so each independent location lands in exactly one segment and the four segments sum to the base.

Key Read: The call order is 1 then 2 then 3: anchors first because they bring management and licensure in place, scarce assets in a sector short of licensed directors, proven brands second for durable local demand, cremation-capable singles third for margin defense as the mix shifts. Segment 4 is half the base: 6,016 locations largely invisible online and least contested, where succession candidates can only be surfaced through direct research.
Source. STOC Advisory operator-segment analysis, August 2026. Operators derived from validated website-domain grouping; the supplied name-frequency location-count field is retained as a legacy column and not used. Segments are mutually exclusive and sum to 11,585.
9
Cremation Economics and Service Signals
62.8% of U.S. Deaths Now End in Cremation, Heading Above 70% by 2033
The disposition shift and the 44.5% of independents already visibly cremation-capable
Part III: The Independent Opportunity
The mix shift is the sector’s core margin story. A funeral with viewing and burial carries an $8,300 median cost against $6,280 with cremation, and direct cremation averages $2,202, with budget providers under $1,000. Disposition disruptors are already in the tracked data (direct-cremation brands After.com, VC-backed, NorthStar’s Smart Cremation, and Foundation Partners’ Tulip, plus human-composting Earth Funeral), concentrated in Western markets where the cremation rate runs highest. Among the 11,585 scrape-observed independents, 5,160 (44.5%) visibly market a cremation offering; nearly every home can arrange one, so the signal measures marketing posture, and the other half faces the shift without visible positioning.

U.S. Cremation Rate, Actual and Projected (% of dispositions)
Solid: actuals (CANA 2026 report: 61.8% in 2024, 62.8% in 2025). Dashed: projections, CANA above 70% by 2033 and NFDA 82.3% by 2045.
Where the Margin Defense Happens
Scale defends cremation margin three ways: owned crematory capacity instead of trade fees (outside the dataset; a first diligence question on every target), pre-need books that lock mix and pricing years ahead, and online arrangement that meets the roughly 30% of consumers willing to arrange fully online. 36% of NFDA-member homes already offer online cremation arrangement. The regulatory floor is rising too: every state requires funeral licensure from January 2027 (Colorado SB 24-173 closes the last gap), and the FTC Funeral Rule remains under an open rulemaking, with mandatory online price disclosure the amendment on the table and no final rule as of mid-2026, a change that would accelerate the price transparency direct-cremation entrants trade on. On the buy side, a target’s pre-need book cuts both ways: trust-vs-insurance structure, funding level, and transferability reprice a deal before any multiple applies.
Key Read: The cremation-visible pool is where consolidation economics work today; the traditional pool is where supply is deepest and least contested. The 16 Group A metros on page 5 concentrate the cremation-visible pool: 1,828 independents in cremation-forward deep pools, in markets where direct-cremation entrants have set the price floor.

Signal counts: STOC Advisory proprietary tracked-location dataset, August 2026. External figures are context only and never combined with proprietary counts.

STOC Execution Framework
From Market Intelligence to a Succession-Sourcing Pipeline
Market selection, owner and decision-maker enrichment, outreach execution, and pipeline tracking aligned to acquisition criteria
Part IV: Execution and Reference
STOC applies the market intelligence through a mandate-specific corporate development workflow. Priority markets, operator segments, enrichment criteria, and outreach are aligned to each acquisition mandate. In funeral homes the sourcing motion is succession-led: owners sell on retirement timelines, and a quality firm that reaches the industry’s broker network draws multiple bidders, so proprietary presence ahead of any process compounds. Two external anchors frame every mandate: deathcare broker benchmarks put quality funeral home transactions at roughly 6x to 8x EBITDA with real estate included, small single-site homes trading well below that, the spread that creates the platform arbitrage, net of integration cost and asset-quality differences; and U.S. deaths ran 3.07 million in 2024, with boomer demographics pointing higher through the 2040s.

STOC Sourcing OS
Sourcing OS is the fund-level infrastructure behind STOC’s Corporate Development Support offering. It brings market mapping, target segmentation, decision-maker enrichment, outreach execution, and pipeline tracking into one system.
Execution Sequence
1
Confirm priority markets

Build the target universe by segment

Launch succession-framed campaigns from the prioritized lists, tailored by geography, operator scale, cremation orientation, and acquisition strategy; retiring owners respond to continuity of name, staff, and community standing; roll-up pitches lose them.

Track responses and pipeline
Capture activity, responses, interest, and pipeline stage in one system; interested owners route to follow-up and market feedback returns to the database.
6
Refine market and segmentation criteria
Use campaign performance and closed-transaction feedback to refine market selection, enrichment rules, and segment definitions across the portfolio.

Methodology Appendix
Methodology, Definitions, and Verification Framework
The notes below establish the denominator, scope, and interpretation used for each analytical component.
TopicMethodology note
Exhibit denominatorsEach exhibit uses the denominator stated on the page. Ownership composition uses all 14,680 location records (12,293 scrape less 9 standalone cemeteries, plus 1,450 roster-added and 946 Texas directory-census records). Depth exhibits (state and metro independent counts, market-group thresholds) include directory-census records; signal-based exhibits (cremation mix, segments, reviews, distances) use only scrape records (11,522 state-assigned; 10,293 CBSA-assigned post-repair; 11,585 total scrape independents). Distance analyses use the 12,093 scrape records with usable coordinates; roster-added records carry no coordinates, reviews, or service signals and are excluded from those exhibits. 935 of 1,450 roster-added records carry a CBSA via city lookup (post-repair).
Texas directory censusTexas held 212 scrape independents against a far larger real base, so all Texas listings were harvested from two national directories (US Funerals Online; Tribute Archive, 1,275 listings), deduplicated on normalized name and city, and filtered of churches, trade services, premises-less referral networks, and standalone cemeteries. Five wide-area cremation brands, each listed under dozens of service towns, were verified on their own websites and collapsed to their single physical sites. After matching against every existing Texas record (297 already present) and setting aside 12 chain-branded listings, the 946 unmatched independents were added (TXDIR-0001..0946) with name, city, state, and CBSA where resolvable; no coordinates, reviews, or signals.
Metro-assignment repairA state-consistency audit found 870 records assigned to metros outside their own state (corrupted source ZIPs; an early city-only lookup). 99 were reassigned via city-plus-state matching, 771 cleared to state totals only, 49 roster and census records gained a metro. A final pass restored the seven leading-zero-ZIP states (CT, MA, ME, NH, NJ, RI, VT), whose ZIPs had lost the leading zero and been right-padded (06401 stored as 64010): recovery and crosswalk re-join assigned 1,187 of their 1,292 records, adding Boston, Providence, and Hartford and completing the New York and Philadelphia metros. Every assignment lies in a member state of its CBSA.
Standalone-cemetery removalA name-pattern review found 13 chain records with cemetery-only names. Four verified funeral-and-cemetery combos were retained (Greenlawn Southwest and Oakmont, Carriage; Holy Sepulchre, CFCS; Arch L. Heady at Resthaven, SCI). Nine standalone cemeteries were removed (four NorthStar, three Everstory, two SCI), most with the parent’s funeral home already recorded in the same city. Independent-side records are unaffected.
Observed vs. known universeNamed-group counts are roster-reconciled: SCI 1,308 vs its reported 1,495, Park Lawn 188 vs ~215, Carriage 132 vs 155 (gaps: cemetery-side directory pages and directory lag; verified combos are retained). Independent counts remain an observed scrape; no census pass was run outside Texas. Only SCI’s capture is roster-testable: the scrape held roughly 190 of its 1,308 tracked locations before reconciliation, which is why the CBP benchmark uses record counts alone. Shares are stated with direction: 85.4% independent is a floor and 14.6% consolidated a ceiling at the tracked groups’ observed footprints. Rosters covered 14 of the 20 groups (2,078 of 2,149 tracked chain locations); the remaining six are scrape-observed with higher company-reported totals (Fidelity 3 vs 40+ properties, Newcomer 30 vs 50+, Heritage 22 vs 110), but reported totals count cemeteries and combos (Everstory: 73 funeral homes of 460 properties), so the gap reaches one point (84.4% independent) only in the extreme case that every reported property is a distinct U.S. funeral home; on the Everstory pattern of roughly one funeral home per six reported properties the adjustment is a few tenths, and the unclosed CBP gap, overwhelmingly independent, runs the other way, so the at-least-85% reading holds on the dataset’s own arithmetic; verified watchlist footprints (largest: an 18-home group) remain classified independent inside the same bound. External estimates near 89% are context only and stay outside the calculation. Record counts are benchmarked against Census CBP 2023 (NAICS 812210; used as a count benchmark only): 14,680 records vs CBP’s 15,183 nationally (96.7%; 93.8% ex-Texas, which now exceeds its CBP count, 1,364 vs 982, since directories include non-employer homes), median state coverage 98%; NFDA and industry estimates put independent ownership near 89% of homes. State and metro shares divide tracked consolidated counts by classified totals; states below 70% of CBP coverage (MI, WI, MO, IA, AK) are flagged in the state table. Top-5 concentration inside the 2,149 tracked chain locations is exact on both sides and a ceiling on true concentration, since smaller groups are scrape-observed.
Roster reconciliationLocation rosters were harvested from company sources (2,143 roster rows: SCI’s complete 1,493-location consumer directory, Carriage’s and Park Lawn’s full directories, and brand and press sources for the rest), matched on domain and on name plus city and state, with collision-rejecting token rules. 466 records originally collected as independent targets were reassigned to their parent groups with per-row evidence (Carriage 96, Park Lawn 95, Everstory 50, Vertin 46, SCI 42, NorthStar 33, Newcomer 29, Milestone 21, and 54 across eight smaller groups); 17 candidate matches were rejected as name-collision false positives. The 1,450 roster locations the scrape had not captured were then added as records (SCI 1,120, Foundation Partners 103, Park Lawn 92, Carriage 35, and 100 across eight smaller groups), after cemetery filtering and de-duplication against every existing record.
Ownership verification frameworkThe 26 named institutional groups are classified from public sources as Verified (primary source), Reported (credible secondary), or Pending. 22 of 26 carry fully Verified or Reported status; a Pending element remains on Foundation Partners’ post-2025 investors, Anthem Partners’ sponsor (a Kensington attribution, unconfirmed), Gibraltar Remembrance’s footprint, and Legacy Funeral Group’s current count. Rows cross-checked August 31, 2026. Independent operators are anonymized throughout regardless of size (named groups are publicly identified acquirers; independents are potential targets); owner and contact information is maintained separately and never appears in the report.
Ownership reclassificationThe supplied ownership vocabulary was remapped to the controlled vocabulary: 239 same-domain family-group rows with unverified sponsors were reclassified to Independent multi-location (a default erring toward independent; any later-verified sponsors sit inside the one-point bound above); SCI, Carriage Services, and Security National were moved to Public Strategic Chain; 25 records on the Altogether brand domain were reassigned from SCI to Foundation Partners Group after brand verification.
Operator groupingOperators are derived from validated website-domain grouping with a name-and-city fallback; brand and roster domains map to their parent groups. The supplied location-count field (normalized name frequency, which merges unrelated operators) is retained as a legacy column, never used analytically.
Market groupsAssigned sequentially so each CBSA lands in exactly one group: Cremation-Forward Deep Pool (50+ classified independents and cremation-visible share at or above 50.0%), Traditional-Mix Deep Pool (50+ independents, share below 50.0%), Mid-Sized Independent (25 to 49), Smaller Observed (all others). Unrounded values are used at thresholds; boundary cases: Chicago (50.1%) in Group A, Virginia Beach (48.6%) and Detroit (48.3%) in Group B.
Operator segmentsFour mutually exclusive segments assigned sequentially: multi-location operators (2+ observed sites), high-visibility singles (100+ reviews and 4.5+ rating), cremation-visible singles, deeper-research singles. Segments sum to the 11,585-location independent base.
Visible service signalsCremation, grief support, memorial, online services, transport, and combo-property indicators reflect visible website and listing signals and do not establish confirmed service revenue mix; they overlap and are never summed as unique locations. Burial and pre-planning flags were collected but excluded as unreliable (observed at roughly 6% against near-universal real-world offerings); the sibling cremation flag is therefore detection-limited too: cremation-visible shares are floors, and metros within a few points of the 50.0% threshold are boundary cases. Crematory ownership (on-site vs trade) was not collected and is flagged as a diligence item.
Excluded supplied fieldsSupplied composite scores and density-varying radii were excluded; transparent rules on stated denominators replace them.
Geography treatmentCBSA assignment uses a ZIP-to-CBSA crosswalk built on the 2018 CBSA delineation via ZCTA spatial join (the supplied metro key assigned 29.8% of records; superseded). Regions are the four Census regions, recomputed from state. Density tiers are the supplied ZIP-population proxy bands; the proxy’s lineage is unconfirmed and its values are binned, so density work is descriptive only. Distances are great-circle (straight-line) miles, never drive time.
External contextIndustry size (IBISWorld, August 2026), funeral home counts and ownership (NFDA, September 2025), cremation rates (CANA May 2026; NFDA October 2025), costs (NFDA 2023 General Price List Study), deaths (CDC/NCHS 2024 final, January 2026), transaction multiples (The Foresight Companies, 2024), and owner retirement (2023 NFDA survey via Bisnow, February 2026) frame the market. External figures serve as separately stated benchmarks, never combined with proprietary counts in any share claim; the 2023 owner survey is read three years on, so part of the reported wave has already transacted.
Source dates. Proprietary tracked-location funeral home dataset: August 2026 (12,293 scrape records; roster reconciliation August 31, 2026). Named-group ownership: public sources as of August 31, 2026 (Named Ownership Appendix). External context: NFDA September and October 2025; CANA May 2026; IBISWorld August 2026; CDC/NCHS January 2026; Census CBP 2023, NAICS 812210 (coverage benchmark), retrieved August 2026.
Basis and limits. All rankings, market groups, operator segments, and signals are derived from the proprietary funeral home location dataset. Ownership classifications for the 26 named institutional groups are supported by cited public sources as of August 2026. Independent operators are anonymized and reported in aggregate. The analysis is not a complete legal-entity census and does not establish call volume, revenue mix, pre-need book size, operating performance, or transaction readiness. Recipients should apply independent judgment and conduct their own diligence.
